title: Fidelity-Latency-Cost Probe (mixed-length workload)
body:
Status: exploratory probe for rmx-7b-ql8 onboarding.
Owner: Ravi Patel (eng-applied-ml).
Summary:
This doc captures a focused probe into latency/cost/quality tradeoffs for a mixed-length production-like prompt set. The goal is to surface practical operating points for initial onboarding and an early rollout plan. Unlike previous sweeps that used synthetic uniform prompt lengths, this test intentionally skews the workload to reflect customer telemetry: many short prompts plus a long-tail of long requests.

Motivation and scope:
- Candidate model: rmx-7b-ql8 (quantized 8-bit variant shipped for evaluation).
- Workload shape: 60% short (<50 tokens), 30% medium (50-200 tokens), 10% long (200-1024 tokens). We observed this distribution in telemetry for three pilot customers.
- Controls tested: batching target (1,4,8,16,32), cache mode (off, prefix-cache, per-client-KV with TTL 30s), and max_tokens cap (64, 128, 256, 512).
- Hardware: Dedicated A100-sim nodes (4xA100 per pool), inference runtime with dynamic-kernel selection.
- Quality metric: promptset-specific F1/EM hybrid (normalized) computed against labeled completion target. Primary quality target: <= 2% degradation vs baseline policy.

Experimental setup:
- Promptset: 4200 labelled prompts (mix of short/medium/long). We partitioned into: 3k short/medium samples for throughput/latency, 1.2k long for stability and cost.
- Warmup: 15 minutes steady traffic per run to populate prefix caches.
- Measurement window: 10 minutes steady-state after warmup.
- Cost proxy: token-cost calculated from observed tokens/sec and inferred per-GPU cost: $0.28/hour per GPU (internal reserved cost). Converted to $/1M output tokens for parity.
- Baseline: batch=1, cache=off, max_tokens=512. Baseline quality=100% (reference).

Key results (representative slices):
Note: numbers are median across 3 repeats. Throughput in tokens/sec, latency in ms, cost in $/1M output tokens, quality as % of baseline.

-- Short-heavy workload slice (60% short):
Batch  | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens | quality
1      | 34      | 78      | 13,200     | 22.1        | 100%
8      | 58      | 190     | 38,400     | 8.1         | 99.8%
16     | 92      | 420     | 44,900     | 6.9         | 99.5%
32     | 160     | 980     | 48,200     | 6.4         | 98.9%

Observations: increasing batch reduces per-token cost significantly for short prompts but p95 climbs rapidly beyond batch=8. Quality impact minimal up to 16, then small regressions at 32 likely due to KV cache eviction timing and tokenization edge effects.

-- Mixed workload (overall distribution):
Batch  | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens | quality
1      | 86      | 230     | 10,900     | 26.8        | 100%
4      | 120     | 310     | 23,700     | 12.4        | 99.9%
8      | 160     | 520     | 35,500     | 8.3         | 99.6%
16     | 230     | 920     | 40,100     | 7.4         | 99.1%

Observations: mixed workloads expose long-request tail that increases p95 across the board. Batch=8 gives a sweet spot for cost without blowing p95 for many customers; p95 ~520ms is borderline for interactive apps.

-- Long-request slice (10% long):
Batch  | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens | quality
1      | 420     | 980     | 1,800      | 160.7       | 100%
4      | 700     | 1,800   | 4,900      | 59.3        | 99.7%
8      | 1,100   | 3,200   | 8,600      | 33.7        | 99.3%

Observations: long requests dominate cost. Max_tokens cap has direct cost impact here (see below).

Max_tokens cap sweep (mixed workload, batch=8, cache=prefix enabled):
Cap  | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens | quality
64   | 120     | 310     | 22,000     | 13.4        | 96.2%  (drops: truncation hurts quality on long prompts)
128  | 140     | 420     | 28,600     | 10.4        | 98.5%
256  | 160     | 520     | 35,500     | 8.3         | 99.6%
512  | 180     | 600     | 37,700     | 7.8         | 100%

Observations: cap <=128 reduces cost but can induce meaningful quality regressions on tasks that require longer completions. 256 looks like a pragmatic compromise for most customers; 64 is only acceptable for very latency-sensitive but low-fidelity use cases.

Cache modes (batch=8, max_tokens=256):
Mode             | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1M tokens | quality
cache=off        | 180     | 620     | 30,200     | 9.8         | 99.7%
prefix-cache     | 160     | 520     | 35,500     | 8.3         | 99.6%
per-client-KV-30s| 145     | 460     | 38,000     | 7.8         | 99.6%

Observations: enabling prefix caching yields ~15-25% cost reduction and improves p50 slightly. Per-client KV with short TTL gives best p95 improvements for conversational scenarios where same-user prefixes repeat shortly. Be mindful of memory footprint.

Stability/regression notes:
- We saw a rare p95 spike correlated with GC pause events on runtime host during batch=32 runs; need SRE follow-up to rule out host-level resource saturation.
- Quality regressions at batch >=32 appear non-random: mismatch in beam search termination for certain tokenization boundaries. Filed JIRA-RINF-1251 to track.
- One outlier customer with 25% long requests will see cost >2x vs median; recommend per-customer capacity sizing or model pinning.

Recommendations (initial onboarding defaults):
1) Canary config (recommended): batch_target=8, adaptive_window enabled, prefix-cache enabled, max_tokens=256, per-client-KV disabled for initial canary (enable selectively). Start at 5% traffic for 48h with strict monitors on p95 latency and quality regression (new promptsets).
2) If canary stable, ramp to 25% over one week. For high-interactivity customers, offer an alternative profile: batch_target=4, max_tokens=128, prefix-cache on.
3) For customers with heavy long-tail (>15% long requests), recommend model pinning to a higher-capacity variant (rmx-13b-ql8) or a dedicated pool with lower batch targets.
4) Operational guardrails: auto-fallback policy to smaller model variant on p95 breach >2x baseline; cost/latency alert when $/1M tokens for a customer exceeds 3x expected.

Open questions / next steps:
- Run same sweep on rmx-13b-ql8 and compare quality gains vs cost uplift (JIRA item created).
- Instrument per-token breakdown across kernel choices to understand where p95 climb originates at high batch sizes.
- Validate results on Dedicated vs Dedicated+NVLink topology (we tested on A100-sim only).
- Add stress test to reproduce GC-related p95 spikes (eng-sre action).

Quick checklist for replication:
- PR to runtime with kernel flags: --adaptive-batch-window, --prefix-cache=true
- Experiment script: tools/eval/run_probe.sh --model rmx-7b-ql8 --batches "1,4,8,16,32" --caps "64,128,256,512" --cache-modes "off,prefix,per-client-30s" --duration 00:10:00
- Data: s3://redwood-evals/probe/mixed-length-4200-v1.jsonl

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an applied probe intended to guide a conservative onboarding default. It's intentionally pragmatic: we prioritize small quality regressions for cost wins, but do not accept regressions >2% on the labeled promptset without explicit product sign-off.
- Please comment on the canary ramping cadence and any additional telemetry you'd want in the rollout dashboard (token-level cost breakdowns, per-prompt quality heatmap, batch composition histogram).

-- Ravi
